strengths: The paper addresses an important problem for multilingual NLP: Wikipedia size and reputation can conceal substantial duplication and contamination. Its broad coverage makes the audit potentially useful for dataset curation.

Separate document and character statistics, together with concrete examples in Table 1, provide credible evidence of placeholders, repeated templates, and mixed-script content. The correlation between MinHash removals and independently estimated bot prevalence (ρ = 0.63) strengthens the descriptive findings.

The evaluation covers 50 monolingual languages and three training regimes, with five-run reporting for several tasks. There are useful positive results, including Cebuano SIB200 improving from 0.39 to 0.51, and many monolingual results remain stable after filtering.

The manuscript is generally well organized, provides extensive per-language results and training hyperparameters, links an open-source toolkit, and acknowledges adverse outcomes and limitations of its evaluation scope.
weaknesses: The central interpretation of filtering rates as data quality is insufficiently validated. The reported 29.36% of documents and 11.68% of characters quantify removal, not independently established low-quality content. Appendix A explicitly removes foreign-script names and references, while templated articles can contain distinct useful facts. A representative human audit of retained and removed content is needed to assess these errors. The four quality tiers also lack sensitivity analysis, and the DEPTH+ correlation of ρ = 0.31 provides only modest corroboration.

A major downstream experiment operates at chance level. In Table 14, both multilingual models average 0.25 on the four-choice BELEBELE task; even English scores only 0.25 and 0.26. Similar performance under these conditions cannot establish preservation of useful reading-comprehension ability. This setup needs diagnosis, a functioning task baseline, and uncertainty estimates before Figure 5 can support the stated conclusions.

The controls do not isolate the effects attributed to data quality. Appendix C trains different tokenizers for raw and filtered corpora, the random baseline matches article count without establishing comparable token exposure, and fixed-epoch training gives conditions different training budgets. These comparisons assess combined pipeline changes. Shared-tokenizer controls, token/compute-matched comparisons, and individual-filter ablations on a representative subset would clarify which changes produce the observed effects.

The broader claims about performance preservation and greater benefits for lower-quality editions need qualification. Table 7's tier averages are unchanged or slightly lower after filtering, with substantial individual losses such as Acehnese's 0.27 to 0.15. Table 13 shows average XNLI performance declining from 0.44 to 0.43. Treating differences within ±5 percentage points as negligible does not establish equivalence, and Tables 12–14 lack reported run variability.

Despite useful hyperparameter tables and the toolkit link, the manuscript omits essential reproduction details: the Wikipedia snapshot and extraction procedure, MinHash shingle and LSH configuration, and the precise clustering configuration. The validation-split construction is also unspecified. These reporting gaps, together with the unresolved quality validation and downstream evaluation concerns, prevent a positive Findings recommendation; targeted experimental and methodological revisions warrant resubmission next cycle.
